Larger versions are still in training: Base-Large (0.5–2T) is 80%+ through pretraining, XL (2–10T) 20%+.

note_tweet.text:
$IREN: Its Real Competitive Advantage Is Taking Shape

The strongest competitive advantage in the AI era is neither superior hardware nor superior software, but the ability to optimize hardware and software together.

The market is still taking a rather crude approach, lumping a wide range of companies together under a single concept. Traditional cloud computing is software-driven, and software development follows the principle of abstraction because differences in underlying hardware performance are relatively small. But AI computing clusters, particularly massive clusters comprising tens or even hundreds of thousands of GPUs, have shattered that abstraction.

For a cloud service provider to gain a genuine competitive advantage in the AI era, building a closed loop of deep hardware control and precise software coordination is one path to establishing substantial differentiation. If a cloud provider lacks sufficient control over its hardware, its software capabilities may not translate into actual performance, or it may be unable to receive the feedback it needs. Therefore, the optimal approach should involve:

Bottom-up feedback: hardware informing software. Physical infrastructure feeds real-time information about power-distribution bottlenecks, network congestion, and node-failure warnings into the cloud-native software orchestration layer.

Top-down control: software adjusting hardware behavior. Based on the priorities of training and inference workloads, software dynamically adjusts power allocation across the cluster, partitions computing resources, and coordinates data storage with GPU scheduling.

This also includes capabilities that require close hardware-software collaboration, such as hardware-level multi-tenancy, network and switch isolation, and physical and logical GPU slicing technologies.

These technical requirements are precisely why new companies have an opportunity to compete on equal footing with established cloud giants in this industry. Software strength alone is not enough, and neither is the hardware strength of traditional cloud providers. In this new era, companies will have a chance to emerge as winners only if they excel at optimizing both hardware and software in coordination.

The AI industry is still in its early stages, and AI infrastructure is still taking shape. The concept of the neocloud remains extremely vague. Does bare metal have the advantage? Does software have the advantage? Neither, on its own. Of course, the market is enormous, and for a considerable period, there will be room for many players to survive. But to become truly competitive in this industry, a company must be strong in both software and hardware coordination.

Infrastructure is undergoing enormous changes. Companies deeply involved in building this new infrastructure will gain advantages in physical facilities. The software capabilities developed on top of that foundation will gradually take shape, purpose-built for the new hardware infrastructure. As a result, they should perform exceptionally well in coordinating increasingly complex systems. I have already seen this trend emerging at the recent GTC conference in Berlin, and it has also been validated by several software capabilities NVIDIA recently developed in collaboration with IREN.

This year, the market has viewed NBIS as having this potential and awarded it a high valuation. NBIS wants to build an integrated, self-contained system, placing particular emphasis on its full-stack software capabilities. However, it cannot match IREN in the scale and depth of its infrastructure deployment. This gap will become increasingly apparent over time, particularly when it comes to individual gigawatt-scale sites. Leasing can make it relatively easy to secure numerous smaller sites quickly, but sites exceeding 300 MW are much harder to secure. Gigawatt-scale sites are effectively out of reach for a leasing-based model.

IREN is building a flagship AI factory for NVIDIA's DSX system. There will be many things that only IREN is positioned to undertake, such as developing individual gigawatt-scale sites, clusters of multiple gigawatt-scale sites located in close proximity, and sophisticated interactions with the power grid. IREN and NVIDIA could well develop multiple reference configurations at different megawatt scales for the market to choose from, ranging from small sites to hyperscale facilities. Throughout this process, IREN is participating extensively in the standardization of AI infrastructure, giving it a strong first-mover advantage in physical infrastructure.

On this foundation, the cloud technology team IREN is assembling will play a critical role, developing software optimized to interact and coordinate with the new AI infrastructure. Throughout this process, its vertically integrated model will prove enormously valuable.

Competition has never been about winning at a single point; it is a massive exercise in system-wide coordination. Even Elon Musk appears underprepared in this regard. His approach of scrambling to pile computing capacity onto gas turbines as quickly as possible may resemble a peacock spreading its feathers: everyone sees the impressive display at the front, but no one notices what is going on behind it. In my view, regardless of whether he can actually pull it off, even if he succeeds, the economics of this approach will likely be very poor. Tesla was built around an uncompromising focus on cost efficiency, but when it comes to AI, that philosophy seems to have turned into spending whatever it takes. I am not convinced by this approach.

As my research has deepened recently, I have come to understand more and more of the decisions IREN has made over the past year. IREN is a deeply involved builder of the AI infrastructure that is now taking shape. By collaborating with leading companies in the AI industry, it is positioning itself as a leader in physical infrastructure, while building a powerful software ecosystem for optimization and coordination on top of that foundation.

For multiple years, I spent the majority of my time focused on the transparency of frontier AI companies. When I was working on that topic, many people asked me why I prioritized this issue. 

Those skeptical of substantial regulation often asked because they believed it was unnecessary. Those supportive of substantive regulation often asked because they believed it was insufficient. For now, I don't want to re-litigate this issue but make a simpler point based on today's events.

The Anthropic S-1 is a wonderful example of the value of  (in this case mandated) transparency into frontier AI companies. It is dispositive on the financial health not just of this one important company, but the industry's financial health, the prospects for its future, and the even broader risks and opportunities society will contend with if/as frontier AI advances forward. 

It should make us think deeply about what disclosures from frontier AI companies will be valuable, and how those disclosures will come to be, especially when the institutional apparatus of the SEC and the federal laws for US corporate finance does not (yet) exist.

We (Jonathan Elkobi, me) are happy that @chinaquarter has accepted our new piece “The End of Fiscal Autonomy. ”  Yes, it’s provocatively titled but this is an important data point for analyzing China’s economy.  A large literature suggests that local autonomy, including fiscal “federalism” has been a key ingredient to growth and local reform initiatives.  If local governments literally have little to no autonomy, their incentives and ability to use local initiatives to generate growth also declines. Below, I summarize our findings with link of pre-pub version at the end. 

Quick primer: Chinese budgeting is broken into 1. ordinary budget to finance public services, civil service salaries and 2. Extra budgetary fund (EBF) used to finance land acquisition/sale, infrastructure projects and other discretionary spend. The source of the problem is here—ordinary revenue at the local level has grown very modestly over a 6-year period (21%), while EBF revenue (land income) has not grown at all due to the property crackdown.  Central transfers made up the bulk of the growth in non-debt sources of income for local governments.  (1/N)

note_tweet.text:
AI companies make safety calls based in large part on internal tests they develop themselves. It’s rare for there to be independent assessment of the quality of those tests.

Earlier this year, @Amazon and @AVERIorg agreed to a pilot project in which AVERI assessed the quality of Amazon’s internal safety evaluations. Today we’re releasing the result of that independent review. As a result of this project, Amazon is changing how it tests future models.

Our review of Amazon’s internal AI safety evaluations confirmed several strengths such as topical diversity, and we found the evaluations to be consistent with Amazon’s public statements on them. At the same time, we found areas for improvement:

On attack sophistication, some prompts represented relatively straightforward attack vectors that would test safety filters rather than deeper model reasoning.

On evaluation signal quality, we identified a concern that superficial cues, rather than safety reasoning, may drive some model refusals, so passing these evaluations might not indicate robust safety behavior in novel situations.
On linguistic and stylistic diversity, some multilingual prompts were included, but prompts across risk categories were predominantly in English, and some prompt structures were reused across scenarios.
On evaluation freshness, a small number of prompts contained temporal references that could become outdated.
In response, Amazon reports four changes for future internal evaluations:

Refreshing its test sets to remove redundant prompts and add more challenging adversarial scenarios;

Introducing a tiered difficulty calibration framework;
Expanding multilingual coverage across all risk categories; and
Establishing a quarterly review schedule to identify staleness and incorporate emerging attack patterns.
Why does this matter? A passing grade on an easy test doesn’t tell us much on its own. As the stakes of AI development and deployment grow, we think that this kind of independent evaluation of internal evaluations (“metaevaluation”) will grow in importance.

We appreciate Amazon opening their internal evaluations up to outside review. We hope more companies take this step to help make their models safer.

While no clear standards exist for metaevaluation yet, @AVERIorg is working to change that. We look forward to sharing more pilot results in the coming months and will continue our work developing standards with institutions like @aievalforum. 

Read AVERI’s full blog post here: https://t.co/KKy2wAgjaI

Read Amazon’s blog post on the collaboration here: https://t.co/UWKSnUjOco

While evaluating Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in a controlled sandbox environment, Cohere's research team observed something unexpected.

Asked to generate a defensive cybersecurity detection rule, the model instead inventoried aspects of the machine it was running on and attempted to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Notably, the model's reasoning trace stated that it would not invoke any tools before taking these actions.

Cohere's sandbox blocked the attempt, and no external communication succeeded. We have not determined the root cause, and we are not asserting malicious intent.

But the incident raises important questions for organizations deploying agentic AI systems: Can models take actions that differ from their stated reasoning, and how should security teams evaluate trust, provenance, and behavior in open-weight models?

We are publishing our findings because organizations making model adoption decisions deserve as much information as possible. We hope this contributes to greater transparency, stronger security practices, and continued collaboration across the AI ecosystem.

Read the full report: https://t.co/TZSugXi2ZE

If they labs want to succeed, the goal of their DeployCo's and (their strategy writ large) needs to be to

1) develop a predictive model that understands which pockets of the economy, at any time, produce the highest returns to frontier intelligence and what those returns are, and

2) build the deployment meta-learner (a continual learning system) that allows them to realize those returns faster, more reliably, and in more valuable areas than anyone else. 

Building/improving 1) tells the labs where to allocate capital (at the limit, compute) and how much to allocate, Building/improving 2) expands the pockets of economic complexity from which they can practically realize returns from allocating machine intelligence (areas of the economy that appear "API complete" to them)

Crucially, 2) provides the ground truth signals that allows 1) to become more predictive over time.

You could optimistically say that developing these capabilities will allow the labs to power positive sum intelligence auctions (to price tokens dynamically in a way that's win, win, win for everyone involved) across the economy. But for variety of reasons (technical, economic, political) I think this is unlikely to work.

The reality instead, is that continuous vertical integration over the (always evolving) distribution of the economy with the highest returns to intelligence—high and increasing task complexity—is the only way they can capture durable value. And these capabilities are what they need to transition to and power this vertically integrated business model.

The labs have realized that selling/provide universal access to frontier tokens AND trying to durably capture value from those tokens (which is required to attract the capital necessary to stay on the frontier in the first place) means continuously competing with your best customers: those that have high returns to frontier tokens.

They know this isn't a coherent strategy and that they need to change course. Selling your alpha to competitors means eroding your long term returns, so you will rationally stop or be forced, by the capital markets, to stop doing that.

(If the logic here is confusing, see @hypersoren's excellent piece below that provides a much clearer, analytical explanation for why you cannot capture durable value by selling tokens. I'm sure, or at least hope, that everyone important at the labs has read and/or understands this.

https://t.co/8euQ0IBy5n)

Ok, so, now that they've decided that this is no longer tenable, and that they need to create and privately monetize machine intelligence via automated capital allocation and deployment capabilities, what does that mean for the rest of us?

Knowing this, the rational move for everyone else is to not fall for the trap of buying from (and in the process) leaking your scarce/singular context to your future competitors (the labs). This is true at the level of individuals, firms, and economies!

Cursor gave us a nice existence proof for what you don't want to happen to the rest of the economy. This supplier, to competitor, to existential threat dynamic was clearest to Cursor first, which is why you saw them post-train their own model first. Unfortunately, in their case, they realized it was already too late, and that the only economically rational decision was to sell to the lab overlords.

They sold because they knew that, in coding, the only only thing standing in the way of the labs getting access to the the scarce context necessary to produce a superior offering was capital. And capital was something the labs of course had in spades. Abundant capital (compute) allowed them to 1) scale pre-training and post training to the point where their coding products were immediately at parity with whatever Cursor could offer, and 2) subsidize tokens such that all of the new context/signal necessary to stay on the frontier/be more useful than Cursor was produced in their harnesses. "Harness / model co-optimization", etc.

Many smart people have extrapolated/generalized this as the likely end state of everything (not just coding), and come to the conclusion that they are better off joining the labs rather than trying to compete with them.

Luckily, lab access to the scarce context necessary to allocate capital / compete / effectively vertically integrate in other areas with high returns to intelligence seems to be more bottlenecked by humans/trust/time than compute/capital, which means that if everyone starts acting in their own best interest, we will make it out of this alive.

(see Dwarkesh's Data Black Hole, Tom Reed's Goodhart Singularity, @anjali_shriva and @joodalooped's RLWD pieces for intuition here)

The labs (not because they are bad people, but because capitalism/markets are a brutal natural selection machine) have of course been finding every way they can to surmount these diffusion bottlenecks, buy themselves more time, obviate these bottlenecks all together, etc. DeployCos, Thrive Holdings, calls to slow development by fearmongering about RSI, data retention under the guise of safety, regulatory capture, are some examples, but there are many more.

We will see their desperation accelerate as open-source catches up to the frontier and as this logic becomes increasingly legible to everyone. You'll see them using capital and aggressive political narratives to try to brute force/coerce these bottlenecks or obviate them. Again this is not because they are bad people, it's just what they need to do to survive.

In other words, the market will work as it should and reallocate capital from the labs to other economic actors, as long as we let it! We mustn't let lab narratives around RSI, existential risk etc. give them the capital, time or political ammunition they need to make the economy look like a central planner or the country look like one with a natural resource curse.

Luckily, particularly in the past few weeks, it seems savvy economic actors are already well aware of what's going on and are finally publicly calling the labs' bluff (with words and capital). 

All of a sudden, everyone is post-training their own models, talking about the importance of an open eco-system and the existential need to own/control your proprietary learning loops (context, evals, selection infra)

CEOs like @satyanadella and @nikesharora are making it abundantly clear that this is existential (and that, of course, they are the ones who can help you!)

And, luckily, many have known this since the beginning. Firms like @formationbio architected themselves from day one (pre-ChatGPT) around proprietary learning loops that they do not rent from others OR rent to others. They instead are architected to monetize their search and learning in ways that cannot be distilled and commoditized. Structuring themselves this way is what will allow them to attract and deploy the capital necessary to provide durable value to the patients they hope to serve!

Even Lilly owns their own cluster, is hiring for 100s of AI related roles (yes, I've been monitoring their job board), and is partnering with the non-frontier lab AI entities that are incentive aligned to provide capabilities without becoming competition.

So we should be alright, if we don't let the psychosis swallow us.
